title: Episode 227: Sweden: The Sunken Flagship Vasa: The Maiden Voyage Disaster of 1628
description:
The tragic and extraordinary story of the royal warship Vasa: built by King Gustavus Adolphus as the mightiest galleon in the Baltic, capsizing in Stockholm harbor twenty minutes into its maiden voyage, and resurrected three centuries later.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we return to seventeenth-century Sweden for one of the most astonishing, tragic, and ultimately miraculous maritime stories in human history: the catastrophic maiden voyage and modern resurrection of the royal warship Vasa.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: GUSTAVUS ADOLPHUS AND THE AMBITION OF THE BALTIC
In the 1620s, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden was transforming his kingdom into a formidable military empire, locked in bitter warfare against Poland-Lithuania. To dominate the Baltic Sea and secure his supply lines to the battlefields of Germany, the king commissioned the most terrifying, heavily armed warship ever conceived in Scandinavia: the royal galleon Vasa. Named after the ruling Vasa dynasty, the ship was intended to be an invincible floating fortress, a psychological weapon that would awe enemies and inspire allies with Swedish naval majesty. Gustavus contracted the renowned Dutch master shipwright Henrik Hybertsson to oversee construction at the royal naval shipyards in Stockholm. Hundreds of skilled carpenters, sawyers, blacksmiths, and ropemakers fell upon the ancient oak forests of Sweden, felling more than one thousand prime oak trees to construct a colossal hull measuring over two hundred feet in length. Henrik Hybertsson unfortunately fell ill and died during construction, leaving the monumental project in the hands of his assistant, Hein Jacobsson. The ambition was boundless, but in the halls of the royal court, political vanity was about to collide with the unyielding laws of physics.  The Skeppsgården shipyard on the island of Stadsholmen was a hive of frantic naval industry, where Dutch master carvers labored alongside local Swedish apprentices to transform Baltic oak into floating instruments of royal power.  Henrik Hybertsson had never built a warship with two continuous gun decks before, relying on Dutch proportional formulas that failed when scaled up to accommodate Gustavus's unprecedented battery of heavy bronze twenty-four-pounders.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE KING'S DECREE: THE FATAL DOUBLE GUN DECK
As construction progressed, King Gustavus Adolphus, writing frantic letters from his military campaigns in Prussia, repeatedly changed his orders for the ship's armaments. Learning that the King of Denmark was building an oversized warship, Gustavus demanded that the Vasa be equipped with an unprecedented battery of sixty-four heavy bronze twenty-four-pounder cannons. To accommodate this monstrous firepower, the shipwrights were forced to construct a second enclosed gun deck high above the waterline, drastically raising the vessel's center of gravity without widening the hull, which had already been laid. Furthermore, Gustavus ordered the ship adorned with over five hundred exquisitely carved, brightly painted wooden sculptures depicting Roman emperors, roaring lions, biblical prophets, and grotesque Polish nobles groveling in defeat. These massive wooden statues, coated in vibrant scarlet, gold leaf, and cobalt paint, added enormous top-heavy weight to the superstructure. When the captain, Söfring Hansson, conducted the traditional stability test in port—having thirty sailors run back and forth across the upper deck—the warship rolled so violently that the test was hastily called off before the ship capsized at the pier. Yet nobody dared tell the impetuous king that his masterpiece was dangerously unseaworthy.  The sixty-four bronze cannons were cast in royal foundries in Stockholm and Örebro, their barrels adorned with the Vasa coat of arms and Latin inscriptions proclaiming the divine right of King Gustavus.  The brightly painted sculptures covering the sterncastle included representations of Hercules and Gideon, meant to portray Gustavus as a biblical and classical hero delivering Protestant Europe from Catholic oppression.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: AUGUST 10, 1628: THE MAIDEN VOYAGE BEGINS
On Sunday afternoon, August 10, 1628, the sun shone brightly over Stockholm harbor as thousands of citizens, foreign ambassadors, and royal officials gathered along the rocky cliffs of Södermalm to witness the Vasa's grand maiden voyage. The atmosphere was electrifying with national pride: flags fluttered from the rigging, church bells rang across the city, and the warship's crew was permitted to bring their wives and children aboard for the ceremonial sail through the archipelago. Under a light south-southwesterly breeze, the Vasa unmoored from the royal palace wharf, was warped along the waterfront, and hoisted four of her massive canvas sails. As the magnificent galleon glided past the fortress of Vaxholm, the gunners threw open the lower gunports to fire a ceremonial salute to the cheering crowds on the shore. For twenty glorious minutes, the Vasa sailed smoothly down the channel, its golden ornaments shimmering in the summer sun, looking every inch the invincible terror of the Baltic.  The ceremonial salute echoed across the granite cliffs of Södermalm, sending plumes of sulfurous white smoke drifting over the water as royal trumpeters on the poop deck played celebratory fanfares.  Hundreds of civilian spectators in rowboats and small skiffs had accompanied the Vasa into the channel, their joyful shouts suddenly turning to screams of panic as the warship began its fatal roll.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SUDDEN GUST OF WIND: CAPSIZED IN MINUTES
As the Vasa cleared the sheltered cliff of Tegelviken, a sudden, moderate gust of summer wind struck the sails from the south. The top-heavy galleon heeled sharply to port. The helmsman fought the rudder, and the ship slowly righted itself as the gust passed. But moments later, a second, slightly stronger gust caught the sails. This time, the Vasa tilted so steeply that the open lower gunports dipped beneath the surface of the harbor water. Waves began cascading through the gunports into the lower gun deck at terrifying speed, flooding the hold with hundreds of tons of seawater in seconds. The heavy bronze cannons, weighing over a ton each, strained against their hemp lashings on the tilted decks. In utter horror, spectators on the cliffs watched the mighty warship heel over onto its side. Within minutes, before the very eyes of the assembled court and weeping families, the pride of the Swedish navy sank beneath the waves into one hundred feet of water, barely thirteen hundred meters from where its voyage had begun, with thirty sailors and family members trapped inside the flooded hull.  Eye-witnesses on the cliffs reported that the warship sank with such terrifying suddenness that sailors in the upper rigging barely had time to leap into the sea before the topmasts disappeared beneath the harbor chop.  Captain Hansson managed to leap from the quarterdeck into the water and was rescued by a passing rowing boat, while several crewmen who had climbed the rigging clung to the protruding mastheads above the water.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ROYAL INQUEST AND THE SCAPEGOAT SEARCH
When news of the disaster reached King Gustavus Adolphus in Prussia, he was beside himself with incandescent rage, writing furiously that the catastrophe must be due to 'recklessness and incompetence' and demanding that the guilty parties be severely punished. A high-level royal commission of inquiry convened at the Royal Palace in Stockholm, chaired by the King's brother-in-law, Admiral Carl Carlsson Gyllenhielm. Captain Söfring Hansson was interrogated under arrest: he swore on his eternal soul that the crew was sober, that the ballast stones had been properly loaded, and that the cannons were lashed tightly. When the court questioned the master shipwright, Hein Jacobsson, he produced the original blueprints approved and amended by the king himself, demonstrating that the hull had been built strictly to the dimensions ordered by the crown. Faced with the awkward truth that the ultimate blame rested upon the infallible monarch's unreasonable demands for double gun decks and excessive cannons, the inquest quietly closed without punishing a single soul. The disaster was officially attributed to 'the will of God', and the sunken galleon was abandoned to the cold, murky mud of Stockholm harbor.  The inquiry revealed that Admiral Fleming had witnessed the alarming stability test in port, yet when asked why he had not halted the voyage, he admitted that he feared the king's furious displeasure more than the sea.  The royal inquest concluded that no living human could be held responsible for the catastrophe, shielding the king's reputation while leaving the sunken warship to be forgotten beneath centuries of harbor mud.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THREE CENTURIES IN THE COLD BALTIC MUD
For over three hundred years, the Vasa lay undisturbed in the pitch-black, frigid waters of Stockholm harbor, buried under centuries of harbor silt. By extraordinary biological fortune, the unique waters of the Baltic Sea saved the vessel from destruction: because of the Baltic's extremely low salinity, the destructive shipworm, Teredo navalis—which devours wooden shipwrecks in other oceans within decades—cannot survive in the Stockholm archipelago. The icy, low-oxygen water acted as a colossal natural refrigerator, perfectly preserving the ancient oak timbers, rigging, sails, wooden statues, and sailors' personal possessions. In the 1950s, an amateur maritime archaeologist named Anders Franzén became obsessed with locating the legendary wreck, studying seventeenth-century harbor maps and dragging the harbor floor with a homemade core sampler. On August 25, 1956, Franzén's sampler struck a solid wooden object near the island of Beckholmen, pulling up a core plug of blackened, ancient oak. The Vasa had been found.  Anders Franzén's persistence transformed underwater archaeology: armed with historical archives and a primitive lead drop-weight, he systematically dragged the murky bottom of the harbor until the weighted corer brought up blackened seventeenth-century oak.  The salvage divers worked in pitch darkness in freezing, sewage-polluted harbor mud, using handheld water nozzles to carve out narrow salvage tunnels beneath the hull with immense courage and skill.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MIRACULOUS RESURRECTION AND THE VASA MUSEUM
Over the next five years, Swedish navy divers performed one of the most daring salvage operations in history, tunneling six passages beneath the fragile wreck using high-pressure water jets and slipping heavy steel cables under the hull. On April 24, 1961, before an international television audience of millions, the blackened oak timbers of the Vasa broke the surface of Stockholm harbor after three hundred and thirty-three years beneath the waves. To prevent the ancient waterlogged wood from cracking into dust upon drying, conservators spent seventeen years spraying the entire hull around the clock with polyethylene glycol, a waxy compound that replaced the water in the wood cells. Today, housed in the magnificent Vasa Museum in Stockholm, the ship stands as the most intact seventeenth-century warship in the world, ninety-eight percent original. Visitors can walk around its towering four-story oak hull, gaze upon its five hundred intricately carved statues, and marvel at the breathtaking paradox of human history: a catastrophic naval blunder that became Sweden's greatest cultural and archaeological treasure.  Today, the Vasa Museum on the island of Djurgården attracts over one million visitors each year, who stand in awe beneath the towering four-story oak stern castle, a preserved monument to seventeenth-century Swedish grandeur and human fallibility.  The preservation of Vasa required nearly four decades of chemical treatments and environmental controls, creating a global standard for the conservation of ancient waterlogged organic artifacts.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our European odyssey travels to the vast plains of Eastern Europe with Episode 228: Poland-Lithuania Part 1—The Winged Hussars, King Jan Sobieski, and the Relief of Vienna in 1683. Until then, stay curious.
